e-625.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given a Velocity Vector
e-625.problem:
The velocity $\mathbf{v}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}(t) = \langle 2t, 3t^2\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(1,2)$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
e-625.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{r} (0)= \langle 1,2 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,(0)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,2⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=1$ and $C_2=2.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}+1,\,{t}^{3}+2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-626.knowledge_point: Calculating a Position Vector Given a Velocity Vector and Time
e-626.problem:
The velocity $\mathbf{v}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $\mathbf{r}=\left\langle 0,\, 0\right\rangle$ when $t=\dfrac{\pi}2,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=\pi.$
e-626.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{r}\left( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) = \langle 0,0 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,0+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=-1$ and $C_2 = 0.$ Therefore, the position is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and the position at time $t=\pi$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -1,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0-1,\,-(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-627.knowledge_point: Finding the Times When a Particle Is at a Certain Location Given Its Velocity Vector
e-627.problem:
The velocity $\mathbf{v}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}(t) = \langle 2t, 1 \rangle\,,\quad t\in(-\infty,\infty).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $\mathbf{r} = \left\langle -1,\, 1 \right\rangle$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times at which the particle is at the origin.
e-627.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $\mathbf{r} = \left< 0,0 \right>.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t,1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 1\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{r} (0)= \langle -1, \, 1 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,(0)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,\,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=-1$ and $C_2=1.$ Therefore, the position is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-1,\,t+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve for the times at which the position is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-1,\,t+1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-1 & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1, \\ t+1 & =0\,⇒\,t=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t= -1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is at the origin.

e-7343.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given an Acceleration Vector
e-7343.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) =  \left<   9\cos {3t},\, \sin{t} \right>.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(0,0)$ and has velocity $\left\langle 2,\,0  \right\rangle$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
e-7343.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{C}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (0)= \langle 2,\, 0 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡0+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,\,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=2$ and $C_2=1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\mathbf{v}(t) = \left<      3\sin{3t} +2 , \,    1-\cos{t} \right>.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+2,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+2\,\text{d}t,\,\int 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+2t+{C}_{3},\,t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{r} (0)= \langle 0,0 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2(0)+{C}_{3},\,0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{3},\,{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_3=1$ and $C_4=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left<  -\cos {3t} + 2t + 1 , \,   t-\sin{t}  \right>.
$$

after.problem:

$$
v(t)=⟨t(6t-4),\,12{t}^{3}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(20,30)$ when $t=2,$ calculate the components of the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$

$r(t)=⟨${{field-1}}$,\,3{t}^{4}-18\,⟩$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t(6t-4),\,12{t}^{3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t(6t-4)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 12{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,3{t}^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(2)=⟨20,30⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2(2)^{3}-2(2)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,3(2)^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨20,30⟩ & =⟨8+{C}_{1},48+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=12$ and ${C}_{2}=-18.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}+12,\,3{t}^{4}-18⟩.
$$

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨t(6t−4),12t3⟩dt=⟨∫t(6t−4)dt,∫12t3dt⟩=⟨2t3−2t2+C1,3t4+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(2)=⟨20,30⟩. Substituting t=2, we get

r(2)=⟨2(2)3−2(2)2+C1,3(2)4+C2⟩⟨20,30⟩=⟨8+C1,48+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=12 and C2=−18. Therefore, the position vector is

r(t)=⟨2t3−2t2+12,3t4−18⟩.

before.html:
Question 2
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v=⟨t(3t−2),8t3⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (30,90) when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t3−2t2+2,t4−24⟩
b
r=⟨t3−t2+2,2t4−42⟩
c
r=⟨t3−t2+2,2t4−24⟩
d
r=⟨t3−t2,2t4−42⟩
e
r=⟨t3−t2+12,2t4−72⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating the velocity gives r(t)=⟨t^3-t^2+C₁, 2t^4+C₂⟩. Using r(3)=⟨30,90⟩ gives 18+C₁=30 and 162+C₂=90, so C₁=12 and C₂=-72. Thus option e satisfies both the velocity and initial position.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v=⟨t(3t-2),\,8{t}^{3}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(30,90)$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t(3t-2),\,8{t}^{3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t(3t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 8{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨30,90⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{3}-(3)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(3)^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨30,90⟩ & =⟨18+{C}_{1},162+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=12$ and ${C}_{2}=-72.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+12,\,2{t}^{4}-72⟩.
$$

Question 2
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v=⟨t(3t−2),8t3⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (30,90) when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t3−2t2+2,t4−24⟩
b
r=⟨t3−t2+2,2t4−42⟩
c
r=⟨t3−t2+2,2t4−24⟩
d
r=⟨t3−t2,2t4−42⟩
e
r=⟨t3−t2+12,2t4−72⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨t(3t−2),8t3⟩dt=⟨∫t(3t−2)dt,∫8t3dt⟩=⟨t3−t2+C1,2t4+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨30,90⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

r(3)=⟨(3)3−(3)2+C1,2(3)4+C2⟩⟨30,90⟩=⟨18+C1,162+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=12 and C2=−72. Therefore, the position vector is

r(t)=⟨t3−t2+12,2t4−72⟩.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e. Differentiating it gives ⟨3t^2-2t,8t^3⟩, the stated velocity, and evaluating at t=3 gives ⟨30,90⟩. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given a Velocity Vector
content.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v=⟨t(3t-2),\,8{t}^{3}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(30,90)$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t(3t-2),\,8{t}^{3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t(3t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 8{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨30,90⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{3}-(3)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(3)^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨30,90⟩ & =⟨18+{C}_{1},162+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=12$ and ${C}_{2}=-72.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+12,\,2{t}^{4}-72⟩.
$$

Question 3
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v=⟨1t+1,−1⟩,t≥0. Given that the particle is at the position (5,2) when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r(t)=⟨2t+1+1,11−3t⟩
b
r(t)=⟨t+1+3,5−t⟩
c
r(t)=⟨2t+1+1,5−t⟩
d
r(t)=⟨t+1+3,8−2t⟩
e
r(t)=⟨2t+1−1,8−t⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives r(t)=⟨2√(t+1)+C₁,−t+C₂⟩. At t=3, 4+C₁=5 and −3+C₂=2, so C₁=1 and C₂=5. Therefore option c satisfies the velocity and initial position.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,-1⟩,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(5,2)$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\sqrt{t+1}+{C}_{1},\,-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨5,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨2\sqrt{3+1}+{C}_{1},\,-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨5,2⟩ & =⟨4+{C}_{1},-3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=5.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t+1}+1,\,5-t⟩.
$$

The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,-1⟩,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(5,2)$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\sqrt{t+1}+{C}_{1},\,-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨5,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨2\sqrt{3+1}+{C}_{1},\,-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨5,2⟩ & =⟨4+{C}_{1},-3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=5.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t+1}+1,\,5-t⟩.
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v=⟨sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (0,0) when t=π2, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨cos⁡t+1,sin⁡t−1⟩
b
r=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩
c
r=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−1⟩
d
r=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−2⟩
e
r=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t−1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating the velocity gives r(t)=⟨−cos(t)+C₁, sin(t)+C₂⟩. At t=π/2, the position is ⟨C₁,1+C₂⟩=⟨0,0⟩, so C₁=0 and C₂=−1. Thus option c is correct.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(0,0)$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-1.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1⟩.
$$

Question 5
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v=⟨sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (0,0) when t=π2, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨cos⁡t+1,sin⁡t−1⟩
b
r=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩
c
r=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−1⟩
d
r=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−2⟩
e
r=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫sin⁡tdt,∫cos⁡tdt⟩=⟨−cos⁡t+C1,sin⁡t+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(π2)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=π2, we get

r(π2)=⟨−cos⁡(π2)+C1,sin⁡(π2)+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨C1,1+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=0 and C2=−1. Therefore, the position vector is

r(t)=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−1⟩.

so we must have C1=0 and C2=−1. Therefore, the position vector is

r(t)=⟨−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−1⟩.

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v(t)=⟨6t−1,t2−1⟩. Given that the particle is at the position r=⟨10,−1⟩ when t=3, calculate the position of P at time t=1.

a
r(1)=⟨43,−6⟩
b
r(1)=⟨43,13⟩
c
r(1)=⟨6,−233⟩
d
r(1)=⟨−12,−233⟩
e
r(1)=⟨−12,−6⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives r(t)=⟨3t²−t+C₁,t³/3−t+C₂⟩. Using r(3)=⟨10,−1⟩ gives C₁=−14 and C₂=−7. Therefore r(1)=⟨−12,−23/3⟩, which is option d.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨6t-1,{t}^{2}-1⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨10,-1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=1.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-1,{t}^{2}-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-1)\,\text{d}t,\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨10,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨3({3}^{2})-3+{C}_{1},\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,-1⟩ & =⟨24+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-14$ and ${C}_{2}=-7.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t-14,\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨3({1}^{2})-1-14,\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}-1-7⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-\frac{23}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v(t)=⟨6t−1,t2−1⟩. Given that the particle is at the position r=⟨10,−1⟩ when t=3, calculate the position of P at time t=1.

a
r(1)=⟨43,−6⟩
b
r(1)=⟨43,13⟩
c
r(1)=⟨6,−233⟩
d
r(1)=⟨−12,−233⟩

r(1)=⟨−12,−6⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector: r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨6t−1,t2−1⟩dt=⟨∫(6t−1)dt,∫(t2−1)dt⟩=⟨3t2−t+C1,t33−t+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨10,−1⟩. Substituting t=3, we get r(3)=⟨3(32)−3+C1,333−3+C2⟩⟨10,−1⟩=⟨24+C1,6+C2⟩, so we must have C1=−14 and C2=−7. Therefore, the position vector at time t is given by r(t)=⟨3t2−t−14,t33−t−7⟩.

To find the position vector at time t=1, we substitute t=1 into the above, and we get r(1)=⟨3(12)−1−14,133−1−7⟩=⟨−12,−233⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Position Vector Given a Velocity Vector and Time
content.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨6t-1,{t}^{2}-1⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨10,-1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=1.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-1,{t}^{2}-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-1)\,\text{d}t,\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨10,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨3({3}^{2})-3+{C}_{1},\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,-1⟩ & =⟨24+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-14$ and ${C}_{2}=-7.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-t-14,\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨3({1}^{2})-1-14,\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}-1-7⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-\frac{23}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2(0)^{3}+{C}_{1},\,\sqrt{(0)^{3}}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-1$ and ${C}_{2}=2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2{t}^{3}-1,\,\sqrt{{t}^{3}}+2⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2(1)^{3}-1,\,\sqrt{(1)^{3}}+2⟩ \\  & =⟨2-1,\,1+2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}

after.problem:

v(t)=⟨2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩.

after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t,\int \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-2$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=\frac{1}{2},$ we substitute $t=\frac{1}{2}$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2πsin⁡(πt),πcos⁡(πt)⟩dt=⟨∫2πsin⁡(πt)dt,∫πcos⁡(πt)dt⟩=⟨−2cos⁡(πt)+C1,sin⁡(πt)+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=3, we get r(3)=⟨−2cos⁡(3π)+C1,sin⁡(3π)+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨2+C1,C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−2 and C2=0. Therefore, the position vector at time t is given by r(t)=⟨−2cos⁡(πt)−2,sin⁡(πt)⟩.

To find the position vector at time t=12, we substitute t=12 into the above, and we get

r(12)=⟨−2cos⁡(π⋅12)−2,sin⁡(π⋅12)⟩=⟨0−2,1⟩=⟨−2,1⟩.

content.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=\frac{1}{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t,\int \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-2$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=\frac{1}{2},$ we substitute $t=\frac{1}{2}$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{t}^{2}+2t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨1,2⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=1.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{t}^{2}+2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int (3{t}^{2}+2t)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨1,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{2(0)}+{C}_{1},\,(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,2⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},\,{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+2⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨{e}^{2(1)},\,(1)^{3}+(1)^{2}+2⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2},\,4⟩.\end{aligned}

Question 10
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v(t)=⟨2e2t,3t2+2t⟩. Given that the particle is at the position r=⟨1,2⟩ when t=0, calculate the position of P at time t=1.

a
 r(1)=⟨2e2,5⟩
b
 r(1)=⟨e2,5⟩
c
r(1)=⟨2e2,4⟩
d
r(1)=⟨e2,4⟩
e
 r(1)=⟨e2,2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2e2t,3t2+2t⟩dt=⟨∫2e2tdt,∫(3t2+2t)dt⟩=⟨e2t+C1,t3+t2+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(0)=⟨1,2⟩. Substituting t=0, we get

r(0)=⟨e2(0)+C1,(0)3+(0)2+C2⟩⟨1,2⟩=⟨1+C1,C2⟩,

so we must have C1=0 and C2=2. Therefore, the position vector at time t is given by

r(t)=⟨e2t,t3+t2+2⟩.

To find the position vector at time t=1, we substitute t=1 into the above, and we get

r(1)=⟨e2(1),(1)3+(1)2+2⟩=⟨e2,4⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Position Vector Given a Velocity Vector and Time
content.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{t}^{2}+2t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨1,2⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=1.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},\,3{t}^{2}+2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int (3{t}^{2}+2t)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨1,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{2(0)}+{C}_{1},\,(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,2⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},\,{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+2⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨{e}^{2(1)},\,(1)^{3}+(1)^{2}+2⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2},\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨0,6⟩$ when $t=0,$ find the times when the particle intersects the $x$-axis. Do not round the answers.

after.worked_solution:
The particle intersects the $x$-axis when its position is $r=⟨x,0⟩,$ where $x$ is arbitrary. So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t-5⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{2}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\,\int (2t-5)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}-5t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨0,6⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+{C}_{1},\,{0}^{2}-5(0)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,6⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=6.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}-5t+6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times when the particle intersects the $x$-axis, we solve for the times at which the $y$-coordinate of the position vector is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-5t+6 & =0 \\ (t-2)(t-3) & =0 \\ t & =2,\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle intersects the $x$-axis when $t=2$ and $t=3.$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨4t,3{t}^{2}-1⟩\,,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-2,0⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times when the particle is at the origin.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4t,3{t}^{2}-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4t\,\text{d}t,\,\int (3{t}^{2}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{3}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-2,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{0}^{3}-0+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-2,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-2$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2{t}^{2}-2,\,{t}^{3}-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2}-2,\,{t}^{3}-t⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}-2=2(t-1)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1, \\ {t}^{3}-t=t(t-1)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1,0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions that satisfy both equations are $t=\pm 1.$ Therefore, we conclude that the particle is at the origin  when $t=\pm 1.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times When a Particle Is at a Certain Location Given Its Velocity Vector
content.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨4t,3{t}^{2}-1⟩\,,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-2,0⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times when the particle is at the origin.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4t,3{t}^{2}-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4t\,\text{d}t,\,\int (3{t}^{2}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{3}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-2,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{0}^{3}-0+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-2,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-2$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2{t}^{2}-2,\,{t}^{3}-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2}-2,\,{t}^{3}-t⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}-2=2(t-1)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1, \\ {t}^{3}-t=t(t-1)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1,0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions that satisfy both equations are $t=\pm 1.$ Therefore, we conclude that the particle is at the origin  when $t=\pm 1.$

before.html:
Question 16
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨0,5⟩.

Given that the particle is at the position (3,−3) and has velocity ⟨1,0⟩ when t=2, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t2+4,5t22+7⟩
b
r=⟨t+4,5t2+72−10t⟩
c
r=⟨t+1,5t22−10t+7⟩
d
r=⟨2t+4,5t2+72−5t⟩
e
r=⟨−t2+t+1,5t22−10t+17⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating a=⟨0,5⟩ and using v(2)=⟨1,0⟩ gives v(t)=⟨1,5t−10⟩. Integrating again gives r(t)=⟨t+C₁,5t²/2−10t+C₂⟩. Since r(2)=⟨3,−3⟩, C₁=1 and C₂=7, matching option c.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨0,5⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(3,-3)$ and has velocity $⟨1,0⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨0,5⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 0\,\text{d}t,\int 5\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{C}_{1},\,5t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨1,\,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{C}_{1},\,5(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,10+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=-10.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨1,\,5t-10⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,\,5t-10⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int (5t-10)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{3},\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(2)=⟨3,-3⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2+{C}_{3},\,\frac{5(2)^{2}}{2}-10(2)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨3,-3⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{3},\,-10+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=1$ and ${C}_{4}=7.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨t+1,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨0,5⟩.

Given that the particle is at the position (3,−3) and has velocity ⟨1,0⟩ when t=2, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t2+4,5t22+7⟩
b
r=⟨t+4,5t2+72−10t⟩
c
r=⟨t+1,5t22−10t+7⟩
d
r=⟨2t+4,5t2+72−5t⟩
e
r=⟨−t2+t+1,5t22−10t+17⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨0,5⟩dt=⟨∫0dt,∫5dt⟩=⟨C1,5t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(2)=⟨1,0⟩. Substituting t=2, we get

v(2)=⟨C1,5(2)+C2⟩⟨1,0⟩=⟨C1,10+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=1 and C2=−10. Therefore, the velocity vector is

v(t)=⟨1,5t−10⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨1,5t−10⟩dt=⟨∫1dt,∫(5t−10)dt⟩=⟨t+C3,5t22−10t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(2)=⟨3,−3⟩. Substituting t=2, we get

r(2)=⟨2+C3,5(2)22−10(2)+C4⟩⟨3,−3⟩=⟨2+C3,−10+C4⟩,

so we must have C3=1 and C4=7. Therefore, the position of P at time t is

r(t)=⟨t+1,5t22−10t+7⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given an Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨0,5⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(3,-3)$ and has velocity $⟨1,0⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨0,5⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 0\,\text{d}t,\int 5\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{C}_{1},\,5t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨1,\,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{C}_{1},\,5(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,10+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=-10.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨1,\,5t-10⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,\,5t-10⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int (5t-10)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{3},\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(2)=⟨3,-3⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2+{C}_{3},\,\frac{5(2)^{2}}{2}-10(2)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨3,-3⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{3},\,-10+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=1$ and ${C}_{4}=7.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨t+1,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\,,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(2,3)$ and has velocity $⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{C}_{3},-t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨2,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨2,3⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=2$ and ${C}_{4}=4.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2+\operatorname{ln}⁡t,4-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given an Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\,,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(2,3)$ and has velocity $⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{C}_{3},-t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨2,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨2,3⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=2$ and ${C}_{4}=4.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2+\operatorname{ln}⁡t,4-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 19
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨6t−2,4⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (0,0) and has velocity ⟨1,4⟩ when t=1, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t3−t2,2t2−2⟩
b
r=⟨2t3−2t2,t2−t⟩
c
r=⟨t3−2t2+4t,t2−2t+6⟩
d
r=⟨t3−t,2t2−2t+6⟩
e
r=⟨t3+4t,t2−t⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration and using v(1)=⟨1,4⟩ gives v(t)=⟨3t²−2t,4t⟩. Integrating again and using r(1)=⟨0,0⟩ gives r(t)=⟨t³−t²,2t²−2⟩, matching option a.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨6t-2,4⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(0,0)$ and has velocity $⟨1,\,4⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-2,4⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨3(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,4⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2(1)^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},2+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=0$ and ${C}_{4}=-2.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨6t−2,4⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (0,0) and has velocity ⟨1,4⟩ when t=1, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t3−t2,2t2−2⟩
b
r=⟨2t3−2t2,t2−t⟩
c
r=⟨t3−2t2+4t,t2−2t+6⟩
d
r=⟨t3−t,2t2−2t+6⟩
e
r=⟨t3+4t,t2−t⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨6t−2,4⟩dt=⟨∫(6t−2)dt,∫4dt⟩=⟨3t2−2t+C1,4t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨1,4⟩. Substituting t=1, we get

v(1)=⟨3(1)2−2(1)+C1,4(1)+C2⟩⟨1,4⟩=⟨1+C1,4+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=0 and C2=0. Therefore, the velocity vector is

v(t)=⟨3t2−2t,4t⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨3t2−2t,4t⟩dt=⟨∫(3t2−2t)dt,∫4tdt⟩=⟨t3−t2+C3,2t2+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(1)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=1, we get

r(1)=⟨(1)3−(1)2+C3,2(1)2+C4⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨C3,2+C4⟩,

so we must have C3=0 and C4=−2. Therefore, the position of P at time t is

r(t)=⟨t3−t2,2t2−2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given an Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨6t-2,4⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(0,0)$ and has velocity $⟨1,\,4⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-2,4⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨3(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,4⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2(1)^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},2+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=0$ and ${C}_{4}=-2.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating x''(t)=48(2t+1)² gives x'(t)=8(2t+1)³+C. Since x'(0)=8, C=0. Integrating again gives x(t)=(2t+1)⁴+D; x(0)=2 implies D=1.
